title: Foraging UK hedgerow fruit in autumn: a seasonal guide
subtitle: Blackberry, sloe, hawthorn, rosehip, and crab apple together
excerpt: From late August through November, UK hedgerows carry five main edible fruits in overlapping seasons: blackberry, sloe, hawthorn haw, rosehip, and crab apple. This guide covers identifying each one side-by-side and planning a hedgerow walk that picks all five in one trip.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); BSBI species accounts for Rubus fruticosus, Prunus spinosa, Crataegus monogyna, Rosa canina, Malus sylvestris; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.
The specific habitat type where a wild plant grows, used as one of the three identification features.

content.text: UK hedgerows in autumn carry five main edible fruits in overlapping seasons: blackberry, sloe, hawthorn haw, rosehip, and crab apple. All five can be found on the same hedgerow walk from late August through November. Apply the
rule-of-three identification
to each species before picking. All five have distinctive features. They share a hedgerow
foraging zone
and can appear on the same stretch of lane.
Seasonal windows
Blackberry: late July through October. First in the hedgerow; finished before the others peak.
Sloe: September through November. Best after the first frosts or two to three weeks of freeze.
Hawthorn haw: late September through November.
Rosehip: August through December. Darkens and softens after frost.
Crab apple: August through October. Best for cooking when firm and fully coloured.
Side-by-side ID
Blackberry: clusters of small black drupelets on a caned shrub with arching thorny stems. Drupelet cluster is the key feature; no other hedgerow fruit has it.
Sloe: small (8 to 12 mm), round, blue-black with a heavy waxy bloom, on an extremely spiny shrub with small oval leaves. Very astringent raw.
Hawthorn haw: round, 6 to 12 mm, deep red, without a sepal crown at the tip. On a thorny shrub with deeply lobed leaves.
Rosehip: oval, 1 to 3 cm, red or orange-red, with a crown of dried brown sepals at the tip. Arching thorny stems with pinnate leaves.
Crab apple: 2 to 4 cm, round, greenish-yellow or red-flushed, on a spiny tree. Cut open to reveal the five-lobed apple core.
Poisonous look-alikes to check
The five hedgerow species above are all fairly distinctive in their fruiting forms. The main dangerous
look-alike plants
to watch for on hedgerow walks:

Deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna): shiny black berries in ones and twos on a large branching plant with soft leaves. Extremely toxic. No thorns, no drupelet clusters. Never touches a blackberry or sloe ID if you check the structure of the fruit.

Black bryony (Tamus communis): red and black berries in string-like clusters on a climbing plant with heart-shaped leaves and no thorns. Often found twined through the same hedgerow. All parts toxic; berries look like miniature rosehips but have no sepal crown and no thorny stem.

Yew (Taxus baccata): red berry-like arils, each containing a single seed, on an evergreen tree with flat dark needles. Seeds are extremely toxic. Not a hedgerow shrub but can appear at hedgerow edges.
Planning a hedgerow walk

A mixed hedgerow walk in October typically yields blackberry (end of season, smaller fruits), rosehips (at their best), hawthorn haws (ripening), sloes (ripe after first frost), and the tail end of crab apple. Bring separate containers for each species; mixing them makes processing harder. Wear gloves for sloes and hawthorn to protect against thorns.
Preparation summary
Blackberry: eat raw, or use in jams, crumbles, vinegar, or wine.
Sloe: freeze first to soften and break the skin, then steep in gin or make sloe jelly.
Hawthorn haw: simmer, push through a fine strainer to remove stones, use in sauce, jelly, or fruit leather.
Rosehip: simmer and strain twice through fine muslin to remove seed hairs; use in syrup or jelly.
Crab apple: quarter, simmer in water, strain. Use in jelly or juice.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of fruit from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Leave at least a third of each fruit on the plant, especially in October and November when birds and small mammals rely on the same hedgerow food sources through winter.

rows.symptom: Cannot tell hawthorn haws from rosehips on the same hedgerow
rows.cause: Both are small and red in autumn; the shrubs may be intertwined
rows.fix: Check the tip of the fruit. Rosehips carry a crown of dried brown sepals at the tip; haws do not. Also check the leaves: haws are on lobed leaves, rosehips on pinnate leaves with separate leaflets.

rows.symptom: Not sure whether a berry is blackberry or something else
rows.cause: Unripe blackberries are red and can look like other small red berries
rows.fix: Only pick fully black blackberries. Confirm the distinctive cluster of drupelets and the thorny, arching caned stem. Red berries on the same plant are just unripe blackberries, not a different species; pick only the black ones.
